2027-07-24.title: Saturday of the ninth week after Pentecost · St Sharbel
readings: With unveiled faces we are being transformed into the image of the Lord
The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head: follow me, and do not look back
2027-07-24.alt: Season of Pentecost, the week after the Ninth Sunday after Pentecost. The Panchangam remembers St Sharbel, the hermit of Lebanon (1828–1898), a saint of the Maronite Church, which like our own Church belongs to the West Syriac tradition.
2027-07-24.verse: all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another;
theo: St Paul puts two meetings with God side by side. When Moses came down from the mountain his face shone, and he covered it with a veil. Paul reads that veil as a sign: the glory on Moses' face was real, but it was passing, and it pointed ahead to a glory that does not fade. He writes as a son of Israel, with grief and love and no contempt; the Church still honours the Law and the Prophets as the word of God, and asks only to read them with Christ in view, for “only in Christ is it set aside.” Then comes the sentence at the heart of today's Epistle: “but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed.” Turning is the whole work of the Christian life. Each morning we turn from our worries, our screens and our small resentments towards the face of the Lord, and as we turn, something is lifted from our eyes.

Paul goes on: “And all of us, with unveiled faces, seeing the glory of the Lord as though reflected in a mirror, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another; for this comes from the Lord, the Spirit.” This is a promise about prayer. We become like what we look at. A child who watches a screen all day begins to talk like the screen; a believer who looks every day at the face of Christ, in the Gospel, at the altar and in the poor, slowly begins to look like him. The change is not our own achievement. It “comes from the Lord, the Spirit,” who works quietly, from one degree of glory to the next, as a monsoon slowly turns a brown hillside green.

Today the Panchangam sets before us a man who spent his life looking at that face. Youssef Makhlouf was born in 1828 in the mountain village of Bekaa Kafra in Lebanon. At twenty-three he left home to become a monk at the monastery of St Maron at Annaya, and he took the name Sharbel, the name of an early Syriac martyr. He was ordained priest in 1859. In 1875, with the permission of his superiors, he went to the small hermitage of Sts Peter and Paul above the monastery, where he lived for twenty-three years in poverty, fasting, silence and prayer. According to his biographers he was stricken with a stroke while celebrating the Holy Qurbono in December 1898 and died on Christmas Eve; Pope Paul VI beatified him in 1965 and canonised him in 1977. His Church, the Maronite Church, shares with our own the Antiochene, West Syriac heritage, and its holy Qurbono is prayed in the same family of ancient rites. His feast is kept on 24 July because 24 December is the vigil of Christmas.

In the Gospel three would-be disciples meet the Lord on the road. To the first, who promises to follow wherever he goes, Jesus says that foxes have holes and birds of the air have nests, “but the Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head”: whoever follows him must be ready for a life whose only security is the Lord himself. To the second he says, “Follow me,” and when the man asks first to bury his father he answers, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but as for you, go and proclaim the kingdom of God.” These are hard words, and they do not despise the fourth commandment; they say that when God calls, nothing may stand in front of him. To the third he says, “No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.” Every farmer in the wet paddy knows that a ploughman who looks back cuts a crooked furrow. Not everyone is called to a hermitage, and the Church does not ask a father, a nurse or a teacher to leave home; but she asks every one of us to put a hand to the plow and not to look back, and to let the Lord come first in the house, the shop and the hospital ward.
outline: Ask: what do I look at most in a day, and what is it making me like?
Point 1 · The veil is taken away
Only in Christ is the veil removed; to turn to the Lord is the whole work of the Christian life.
Beholding the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, we are transformed from one degree of glory to the next.
Point 3 · St Sharbel, hermit of Annaya
Twenty-three years of silence and the Holy Qurbono: a life turned to the Lord.
The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head; whoever follows him does not look back.
live: Tomorrow morning, before you touch the phone, spend two minutes in silence before a crucifix or an icon and say: Lord, I turn to you.
This week set aside one half hour, early morning or late evening, with no screen and no talk, and give it to the Lord in the spirit of St Sharbel.
Name one thing the Lord is asking of you that you keep postponing, and take its first step before Sunday.
2027-07-24.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, you are the glory of the Father and the face in which we see him. Take away the veil that lies over our hearts, and turn our eyes to you every day. Through the prayers of St Sharbel, who sought you in silence and in the Holy Qurbono, teach us to love prayer, to follow you without looking back, and to be changed from one degree of glory to another by your Holy Spirit. You live and reign with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
altar: St Sharbel prepared for the Holy Qurbono with long prayer and gave it the best hours of his day; at the altar the veil is lifted for all of us, for there the Lord who was hidden in Moses' cloud gives himself to be seen in faith, under the signs of bread and wine, as his Body and Blood.
conn: 2 Corinthians 3:13 looks back to Exodus 34:33–35: “When Moses had finished speaking with them, he put a veil on his face”; he lifted it whenever he went in before the Lord, and Paul sees in this the pattern of turning to the Lord.

2 Corinthians 4:6: “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ”; the hermit's whole life is a gaze towards that face, and Matthew 5:8 promises that “the pure in heart” will see God.

Luke 9:61–62 recalls 1 Kings 19:19–21, where Elijah calls Elisha from the plow; Elisha asks to kiss his father and mother, and then follows; the Lord of the Gospel asks for an even more undivided following. The Panchangam remembers Elijah the Prophet on 20 July.
fathers: Love silence above everything, for it brings a fruit that the tongue cannot describe; at first we must force ourselves to love it, but afterwards a joy is born from it which draws us on (Ascetical Homilies, in substance).
You have made us for yourself, O Lord, and our heart is restless until it rests in you (Confessions 1.1, in substance).
magis: Hermits, without always professing the three evangelical counsels, devote their life to the praise of God and the salvation of the world through a stricter separation from the world, the silence of solitude, and assiduous prayer and penance (in substance).
Contemplation is a gaze of faith fixed on Jesus: a farmer of Ars used to say before the tabernacle, “I look at him and he looks at me”; this gaze is a renunciation of self (in substance).
Contemplative prayer is silence, the symbol of the world to come, or silent love; in it words are not speeches but twigs that feed the fire of love (in substance).

quick: St Paul says that when we turn to the Lord the veil is removed, and with unveiled faces we are changed into his image.
St Sharbel, a Maronite monk of Lebanon, lived twenty-three years as a hermit in prayer and silence and loved the Holy Qurbono above all.
Jesus says that no one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.
2027-07-24.action: Spend two minutes in silence before the cross today, with the phone out of reach.
2027-07-24.question: What do I look at most in a day, and what is it making me like?

family.explain: Jesus asks us to follow him all the way. A farmer who is ploughing a straight line must keep his eyes ahead, not behind. Today we remember St Sharbel, who lived on a mountain in Lebanon, praying and working in silence, so that his heart looked only at Jesus. We cannot all live on a mountain, but we can all look at Jesus every day, in our prayers, at church and in the people around us.
family.intention: We pray for monks, nuns and all who live a quiet life of prayer for the world.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing I can do today that keeps my eyes on Jesus?”

illus: A young engineer in Kottayam told his parish priest that he could not pray: his mind jumped from one thing to another and the ten minutes felt like an hour. The priest gave him a simple task. Every morning, with the phone left in another room, he was to sit before the picture of the Sacred Heart in his house and do nothing but look. For weeks it was boring. Then one evening his mother, passing the door, stopped and said, “You sat just like your grandfather used to when he came back from Qurbono.” He had not noticed that he had started to carry himself the way the old man did. Looking had begun to change him.

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you are the glory of the Father. Remove the veil from our hearts, and through the prayers of St Sharbel teach us to turn to you each day. Amen.
share: When one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (2 Corinthians 3:16). What veil lies over my heart today?
We are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another (2 Corinthians 3:18). Where have I seen the Lord change me or someone I know?
No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). What am I tempted to look back at?
pm.resp: Lord, turn our hearts to you.
interc: For the Church, that she may turn to the Lord with unveiled face and be changed into his image.
For monks, nuns and hermits of every Church, that their prayer in silence may be a blessing to the whole world.
For the Maronite Church and all the Eastern Churches that share our Syriac heritage, in communion with the Church of Rome.
For young people who are being called, that they may hear the voice of the Lord and follow him without looking back.
For the sick and the lonely, that they may know that the Lord has made his home with them.
pm.close: Father, you drew your servant Sharbel to a life hidden in silence, prayer and the Holy Qurbono. Turn our hearts to your Son, that we may be changed into his image, and keep us faithful in following him to the end. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

term: A hermit is a Christian who, with the approval of the Church, lives alone in silence, prayer and penance for the praise of God and the salvation of the world. The Church recognises this way of life (Catechism 920); in the Syriac tradition it has an old and honoured place, from the monks of the Syrian desert to the hermits of the mountains of Lebanon.
kidsaint: When Sharbel was a boy named Youssef, he looked after the family's cattle on the mountain. While the animals grazed, he would go into a little cave nearby and pray. The other children played, and he prayed; he was not unkind or proud, he simply loved to talk to God. When he grew up, he became a monk and then a hermit, and the whole of his life was a long prayer. Lesson: you can talk to Jesus anywhere, even while you mind the cows.

homily: Dear friends, today St Paul tells us that there is a veil over our hearts that only Christ can lift: when one turns to the Lord, the veil is removed (2 Corinthians 3:16). Moses covered his shining face with a veil; but we, with unveiled faces, see the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, and we are changed into his image. We become like what we look at, so what are we looking at?

The Panchangam remembers St Sharbel, a Maronite monk of Lebanon. He left home at twenty-three, became a monk, then a priest, and for twenty-three years lived as a hermit above the monastery of Annaya, in poverty, fasting and prayer. He was stricken while celebrating the Holy Qurbono and died on Christmas Eve 1898. Pope Paul VI canonised him in 1977. His Church belongs, like ours, to the West Syriac family.

In the Gospel Jesus asks for a following that does not turn back. The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head (Luke 9:58). No one who puts a hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God (Luke 9:62). Few are called to a hermitage, but everyone is called to keep the Lord first.
So let us turn to the Lord every morning, give him a quiet half hour in the week, and finish what we have begun in his name. Let us not look back. Amen.
kids: Children, have you ever walked in the wet rain with your umbrella and looked at the puddles? You see your own face in the water as in a mirror. St Paul says that when we look at Jesus, it is like looking into a mirror that makes us look more and more like him. St Sharbel loved to look at Jesus in prayer, so much that his whole life shone. Every day, say a little prayer and look at the cross. Jesus will make your heart shine too.

intro: Theme: “With unveiled faces … we are being transformed.”
On Saturday of the ninth week after Pentecost, with St Sharbel: the veil taken away in Christ, the hermit of Annaya, and the plow that does not look back.

sub: Moses' shining face and the veil.
Only in Christ is it set aside.
Turning to the Lord every day.
q: the Israelites would see the face of Moses, that the skin of his face was shining;
For it is the God who said, “Let light shine out of darkness,” who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ.
points.apply: Each morning this week, turn to the Lord for two minutes before you look at anything else.

sub: We become like what we look at.
The mirror of the Gospel and the altar.
From one degree of glory to another.
q: Look to him, and be radiant; so your faces shall never be ashamed.
but be transformed by the renewing of your minds
points.apply: Choose one thing you look at too much and give its time to the Gospel this week.

points.h: St Sharbel, the hermit of Annaya
sub: From Bekaa Kafra to the monastery of St Maron.
Twenty-three years in the hermitage of Sts Peter and Paul.
A Syriac saint who loved the Holy Qurbono.
q: Be still, and know that I am God!
In the morning, while it was still very dark, he got up and went out to a deserted place, and there he prayed.
points.apply: Give a quiet half hour this week to prayer, without a screen.

points.h: The plow that does not look back
sub: The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.
Keeping the Lord first in a family and a job.
q: Then he set out and followed Elijah, and became his servant.
forgetting what lies behind and straining forward to what lies ahead, I press on toward the goal
points.apply: Take the first step this week on one thing the Lord has asked you to do and you have postponed.

concl: When we turn to the Lord the veil is removed, and looking at him changes us into his image.
St Sharbel gave twenty-three years of silence to that gaze; every disciple gives the Lord the first place and does not look back.
2027-07-24.resolve: Turn to the Lord every morning, give him a quiet half hour, and keep your hand on the plow.
